title: Project introduction and strategic questions
text: 1.1. Business problem # In the Iranian labor market, a job posting does three things at once: it announces the employer's demand, it shows the employer's expectation level for skills and experience, and, when salary is declared, it reveals the offered price of labor. Aggregated over time, these postings build a quantitative picture of “who hires whom, with what skills, where and at what price”. JobVision, as one of Iran's largest job platforms, has published its posting data publicly. This data offers a rare opportunity for labor market analysis, but it is raw: 43 columns of different types, free Persian text, JSON structures, missing values and one fundamental limitation — only about one third of postings declare salary. The goal of this project is to turn this raw data into actionable insight for three audiences: HR manager or business owner: With what salary and benefits should we hire? When and under what conditions should we publish the posting? Which skill really adds value? Job seeker: Which skill, degree, experience and geography yields the highest financial return? How large is the gender and provincial gap? Policymaker and labor market analyst: In which seasons does demand peak? Which sectors are growing or shrinking? How has geographic concentration changed? 1.2. Our role in this project # We act as JobVision's data analysis team. The CEO and HR manager of a fictional company, “Robehrashd”, have asked us to deliver a documented picture of the market before drafting next year's hiring plan. So every analysis must be tied to one of these decisions: whom should we hire, at what price, at what time and under what conditions? 1.3. Four management questions # The project brief raises four high-level questions. These questions are broken down into measurable indicators so that the answers can be checked and rejected or confirmed. text: This section builds the analysis infrastructure and runs once and for all. All tables are displayed through one function ( show_table ), all key numbers through one template ( show_metrics ) and all figures in one colour style, so that the reader does not become confused between sections. fa prepares Persian text for display in figures (letter shaping and right-to-left order). RTLTable and show_table display a table with its number, title, sample and period, keeping each column's unit in its header. MetricBlock and show_metrics isolate the key numbers of each section so that they can be referenced in the text. AnswerText and show_answer present the final answer to each question with numeric evidence. complete saves a figure under a unique number in outputs/figures/ and displays it in the notebook; these same files are used in the PDF report. The middle layer is the body of the administrative, sales and services labor market; the layer above 20 million, which accounts for less than one ninth of postings, belongs to specialized, engineering and managerial roles. The type of declared range also reveals a managerial pattern: no posting declared a range narrower than 15%; that is, Iranian employers almost always build a negotiation margin of at least 15 percent into the posting. This is itself a practical recommendation: if you want the posting to look more professional, declare a range of about 20 to 25 percent — not a narrow range that only shows the expectation ceiling, and not a very wide range that leads to the posting losing credibility. 6.2. The 2.4 million gap between the mean and the median is itself the best evidence that the “mean” is misleading in this data; a manager who takes the market mean as the salary basis would offer above the market for half of the roles. For this reason, the median and quartiles are reported in all sections. Taking the logarithm makes the distribution approximately normal (skewness falls from 2.68 to 0.43), and this is the technical justification for using the logarithm of salary as the target variable in section 16. The distribution of hourly income is also skewed but its range is narrower: median 63.5 and the 99th percentile about 300 thousand tomans per hour. Requested work experience is also skewed: median 2 years, third quartile 3 years, and 15.8% of job postings need no experience; in contrast, only 732 job postings ask for more than 10 years of experience. The overall picture is that Iran's labor market is a “low-experience” market: it usually wants fresh workers or those with two to three years. Figure 7.4 shows that the experience distribution is concentrated at 0 to 3 years and thins out quickly after 5 years; this same pattern is examined in section 8 as a clue to the diminishing returns of experience. 7.2. Pearson and Spearman correlation matrix # Table 8.1 | Twelve variable pairs with the largest absolute Pearson correlation | 116,244 postings with salary and hours Pearson Spearman Difference Variable pair Monthly hours — weekly hours 1.000 1.000 0.000 Median salary — hourly income 0.633 0.864 0.231 Hourly income — monthly hours -0.535 -0.409 0.127 Hourly income — weekly hours -0.535 -0.409 0.127 Required experience — median age 0.398 0.373 -0.025 Median salary — required experience 0.394 0.376 -0.018 Number of benefits — company size 0.311 0.316 0.005 Hourly income — required experience 0.216 0.272 0.055 Median salary — median age 0.212 0.216 0.004 Required experience — skill count 0.194 0.245 0.051 Median salary — number of benefits 0.148 0.177 0.029 Required experience — company size 0.125 0.166 0.041 Note: A notably positive difference means the rank relationship is stronger than the linear one (a sign of non-linearity). Interpretation of figures 8.1 and 8.2 and table 8.1: The strongest relationship is the negative relationship between weekly hours and hourly income (−0.68), which is partly mechanical: hourly income is constructed by dividing salary by hours. More important is the difference between Pearson and Spearman for the “salary–hourly income” pair (0.44 versus 0.69); this difference shows that the relationship between these two variables is non-linear and that the ranks are more aligned than the linear values. Work experience correlates with salary at 0.40; no variable alone explains more than 0.5 of the variation in salary. This is itself a finding: salary is not a single-factor variable but a combination of job, skill, geography, company size, and experience. That is why the multivariate model in section 16 is necessary. Interpretation of table 8.2: The variance inflation factor for all numeric variables is below 1.5, meaning there is no serious multicollinearity. This result is somewhat counterintuitive, since experience and age, or company size and the number of benefits, would usually be expected to overlap; but in this data the correlations are mild and each variable carries relatively independent information. Therefore the coefficients of the ridge model in section 16 are interpretable. Limitation: this test was performed only on numeric variables and does not cover categorical variables. 8.2. text: 16.1. Model design # The goal is to predict the log of the median salary range from job, skill, location and organisational features. We take the logarithm because the salary distribution is skewed (Section 7). The base model is ridge regression with standardised features, so that coefficients are comparable across variables. We train a separate model for each year to see how the determining factors have changed over time. text: Question: which job titles are close to one another in terms of their “skill and education basket”? To answer, we turn each job title into a vector: the share of that title's postings that request each skill, together with the share of postings requiring a master's degree or higher. We then cluster the titles. Key figures: clustering data Titles with at least 50 postings: 762 Covered postings: 254,451 (70.7%) Skills in the vector: 40 Vector dimensions per title: 42 Interpreting the clustering data: 762 job titles with at least 50 postings were selected, covering 70.7% of postings overall (254,451 postings). The vector of each title has 42 dimensions: the share of 40 frequent skills, the share of master's degrees and median experience. Before clustering, the skill vector is weighted with TF-IDF so that ubiquitous skills (Excel and Word) do not take over the whole space — without this step, all titles would fall into one giant cluster. 17.1. Interpreting Table 17.1 and Figures 17.1 and 17.2: The silhouette criterion selects k=3 with a score of 0.510. The two-dimensional map shows that the space has one large “general mass” and two “specialist islands”; not several clusters of equal size. This is itself a finding: at the skill level, Iran's market of job titles does not have high cluster diversity, and a large part of the roles is run with one shared skill basket (office software + administrative communication). 17.2.
